title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
authors: Robin Harper, Xanda C. Kolesnikow, Campbell K. McLauchlan, Georgia M. Nixon, Stephen D. Bartlett, Benjamin J. Brown
abstract: We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.
summary: This paper reports on achieving high-fidelity logical qubit operations on a superconducting quantum processor using surface codes. The researchers utilized advanced error correction techniques, including defect exclusion and fast resets, to suppress errors. They successfully demonstrated complex quantum information tasks like entanglement generation and state teleportation across multiple logical qubits.
main_problem: The primary goal is to demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computation on a physical hardware platform.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated logical entanglement (Bell state fidelities > 93%) and performed state/gate teleportation using three logical qubits, while maintaining low logical error rates (< 1%) through advanced error correction.
method: The work employs Quantum Error Correction (QEC) using surface codes, combined with advanced techniques like defect exclusion, fast hardware resets, and lattice surgery protocols.
model_or_system: The experiment is performed on a superconducting quantum processor, specifically the 'ibm phoenix,' which utilizes a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits.
key_observables: Logical error per round, logical Bell-state fidelities, and the decay rate of error probability over many syndrome measurement rounds.
important_parameters: Code distances (3 and 5), logical error rates below 1%, and stability improvements approaching $10^{-7}$ over 170 rounds.
main_assumptions: Performance relies heavily on defect exclusion techniques to mitigate underperforming physical qubits, and fidelity measurements sometimes rely on bounds derived from expectation values due to readout limitations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the placement of surface codes, the results of lattice surgery for Bell state creation and teleportation across three qubits, and stability plots comparing error rates with and without fast hardware resets.
paper_structure: The paper details the implementation of QEC on the superconducting chip, progresses through demonstrating basic logical memory, and culminates in complex protocols for multi-qubit entanglement and state/gate teleportation using lattice surgery.
why_interesting: The rigorous experimental demonstration of fault-tolerant protocols, especially the incorporation of hardware-specific mitigation like fast resets and defect exclusion, provides crucial benchmarks for scaling quantum computation.

Here we show stabilizers of the lower stability experiment (B) and highlight the location of A. The walking circuit moves between these two locations. FIG. 5. Crosstalk between logical qubits. (Top.) Place- ment of two distance-3 logical qubits operated simultaneously, but independently. Logical qubit A is being operated with qubit 55 removed, using the techniques described in section B. (Bottom.) The per-round error is the logical error per round when the logical qubits are operated simultaneously. The number in brackets is the increase in the logical error rate (in percentage points) compared with operating the logi- cal qubits individually. Lift is the ratio of the probability that one logical qubit has an error given an error on the other, to its unconditional error probability.
